title: An Illustrated Explanation of the Ten Dharma Realms
author: Compiled and annotated by Zhanran
excerpt: Ordinary and sage alike never leave the one mind; good and evil are both created by the mind.

inline.s: Ordinary and sage alike never leave the one mind; good and evil are both created by the mind.

[The ten dharma realms] Abbreviated as the ten realms, namely: the hells, hungry ghosts, animals, asuras, humans, devas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and Buddhas. The first six are the six ordinary states, and the last four are the four sages.
A verse says:
Three dots appear like stars, one hook slanted like the moon;
The fur-clad beasts come forth from it, and becoming a Buddha also comes through it.

The first two lines of the verse depict the character for “mind” (xin); the “mind” here is what was said above — “the discriminating, knowing mind present in our daily use,” that is, the mind of the present single thought. “Wearing fur” means becoming an animal.
The Sutra of the Ten Wholesome Ways of Action says:

“Because the thoughts of all sentient beings differ, the karma they create differs as well, and from this arise the revolving rebirths among the various destinies. O Dragon King, do you see this assembly
(the Buddhas, great bodhisattvas, great bhikshus, devas, humans, and asuras in this assembly)
, and in the great sea, the many beings of different forms and colors and kinds? All of these, without exception, are created by the mind,
(all are created by the mind),
brought about by wholesome and unwholesome karma of body, speech, and mind.”
The “Ten Dedications” chapter of the Avatamsaka Sutra
says in verse: “All that exists in the world, with its manifold and varied retributions, is brought to completion by the power of karma.”

[Karma] All our wholesome and unwholesome thoughts, words, and deeds are called karma; wholesome thoughts, words, and deeds are called “wholesome karma,” and unwholesome thoughts, words, and deeds are called “unwholesome karma.” [The power of karma] The force of karma. Wholesome karma has the power to produce pleasant results, and unwholesome karma has the power to produce painful results.
The Sutra of the Five Sufferings Spoken by the Buddha says:

“It is the mind that seizes the hells, the mind that seizes hungry ghosts, the mind that seizes animals, the mind that seizes devas and humans; whatever forms are fashioned, all is done by the mind. One who can subdue the mind and take it as the way has the greatest power. I struggled with the mind for countless kalpas, and only now have attained Buddhahood and walk alone through the three realms — all of it the work of the mind.”
The Sutra of the Contemplation of the Mind-Ground of the Great Vehicle says:
“The Buddhas take the Dharma as their great teacher, and by cultivating the mind realize the path of bodhi.”
The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:
“Simply use this mind, and directly become a Buddha.”
The Zongjing Lu (Record of the Mirror of the Source) says:
“Becoming a Buddha is never
(not)
apart from the present thought.”
An ancient worthy said:
“If the wild mind does not rest, the moment it rests is bodhi.”

blocks.text: The Buddha's Diagram of the Ten Dharma Realms Explained (Diagram)

inline.s: In this diagram, at the center of the ten dharma realms is the “mind,” showing that whichever dharma realm one ultimately finds oneself in is brought about entirely by the workings of the mind — hence the saying “the ten realms are only the mind.”
The Avatamsaka Sutra says:
“If one wishes to understand all the Buddhas of the three times, one should contemplate the nature of the dharma realm: everything is created by the mind alone.”
The Sutra of the Ten Wholesome Ways of Action says:

“Because the thoughts of all sentient beings differ, the karma they create differs as well, and from this arise the revolving rebirths among the various destinies. O Dragon King, do you see this assembly
(the Buddhas, great bodhisattvas, great bhikshus, devas, humans, and asuras in this assembly)
, and in the great sea, the many beings of different forms and colors and kinds? All of these, without exception, are created by the mind,
(all are created by the mind),
brought about by wholesome and unwholesome karma of body, speech, and mind.”

[The Buddhas of the three times] The three times are past, present, and future. The Buddhas of the past are Kāśyapa and the other Buddhas; the Buddha of the present is Śākyamuni Buddha; the Buddhas of the future are Maitreya and the other Buddhas. These are the Buddhas of the three times spoken of in the sutras.
The text for each realm in the diagram is as follows:
The mind of a Buddha: the whole dharma realm is one mind; the three kinds of enlightenment are perfected in practice; the myriad virtues are complete.
The mind of a bodhisattva: keeping in mind the benefit of others, broadly cultivating the six perfections, and walking the middle way.
The mind of a pratyekabuddha: awakening to the twelve links of dependent origination, realizing that all is empty, and delighting in solitude and quiescence.
The mind of an arhat: practicing the path of the Four Noble Truths, knowing suffering, cutting off its cause, aspiring to cessation, and cultivating the way.
The mind of the deva realm: the five precepts and ten wholesome deeds, cultivating virtue with a kind heart, guarding the country and blessing the people.

The mind of the human realm: firmly upholding the five precepts; where they are complete there is wealth and honor, where they are lacking there is poverty and lowliness. (Wealth, honor, poverty, lowliness.)
The mind of an asura: equal to devas in precepts and good deeds, yet haughty and envious in heart, jealous and quarrelsome.
The mind of an animal: ignorant and off the way, without propriety, bent only on their own affairs, running amok and acting by force. (Born from womb, egg, moisture, and transformation.)
The mind of a hungry ghost: stingy and greedy, taking what is not given, stealing unjustly; their blessings are spent and their vital energy exhausted.
The mind of a hell-dweller: violent and ignorant, defying superiors and bullying inferiors, brutal, rebellious, and perverting reason. (Cauldrons of oil, pillars of bronze, mountains of knives.)

[The ten dharma realms] The hells, hungry ghosts, animals, asuras, humans, devas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and Buddhas. The first six are the six ordinary states, and the last four are the four sages. [The three kinds of enlightenment] Self-enlightenment, enlightening others, and the perfection of enlightening practice. Self-enlightenment is causing oneself to awaken, but one must cut off entirely the delusions of views and thoughts within the three realms and the delusions as numerous as dust and sand and the fundamental ignorance beyond the three realms before one can be said to have reached the stage of self-enlightenment. Enlightening others is transmitting to others the truth one has awakened to, so that they too may awaken. The perfection of enlightening practice means that the degree of one's enlightenment has reached the ultimate and perfect state.

blocks.text: The Ten Realms Are Only the Mind

inline.s: On “the ten realms are only the mind,” Master Hanshan taught in the Collection of Dream Wanderings, in “Instructions to Xu Qingzhi”:

[The Buddha said: “The dharmas above and below the three realms are all made by the one mind alone.” What is above the three realms are the four world-transcending sages, namely the Buddhas, bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas. What is below the three realms are the ordinary beings of the six paths, namely the three good paths of devas, humans, and asuras, and the three evil paths of hells, animals, and hungry ghosts. Thus, within the ten dharma realms, all sages and ordinary beings, all good and evil causes and effects, and the adornment of both the circumstantial and the direct retributions,
are all created by the one mind
. Yet this one mind is nothing else,
but the discriminating, knowing mind present in our daily use

The Buddha said: all dharmas above and below the three realms are made by the one mind alone. What is above the three realms are the four world-transcending sages: the Buddhas, bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas. What is below the three realms are the ordinary beings of the six paths: the three good paths of devas, humans, and asuras, and the three evil paths of hells, animals, and hungry ghosts. Therefore, within the ten dharma realms, all sages and ordinary beings, all good and evil causes and effects, and the adornment of both the circumstantial and direct retributions, are all created by the one mind. Yet this one mind is nothing else but the discriminating, knowing mind present in our daily use.

[The ten realms] The ten dharma realms, namely: the hells, hungry ghosts, animals, asuras, humans, devas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and Buddhas. The first six are the six ordinary states, and the last four are the four sages. [The circumstantial and direct retributions] The circumstantial retribution and the direct retribution. The lands, houses, utensils, and so forth of the world, upon which the body depends, are called the “circumstantial retribution”; the body of a sentient being, a temporary combination of the five aggregates, which is the response to past karma, is called the “direct retribution.” [Adornment] The word “adornment” here means decoration. To adorn a land with goodness and beauty, or to adorn the body with merit and virtue, is called adornment; to accumulate evil deeds upon the body is also called adornment. For example, the Sutra of Amitābha Spoken by the Buddha says: “adorned with merits and virtues.” The Sutra of the Contemplation of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life says: “Such a fool steals the property of the Sangha, robs the possessions of the present Sangha, preaches the Dharma impurely, and is without shame or remorse, adorning himself with all manner of evil karma.”
[The mind]

In Buddhist studies the term “mind” is used extremely widely and carries many meanings, so one must be clear about what “mind” refers to in a given passage; otherwise an error of a hair's breadth leads to a mistake of a thousand miles. Here Master Hanshan clearly points out that the “mind” in “the ten realms are only the mind”
is the discriminating, knowing mind present in our daily use

[The three realms] The realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm. The realm of desire is the world inhabited by beings who have the two desires of lust and food, encompassing upward the six desire-heavens, in the middle humans and animals, and downward to hungry ghosts and hells. The realm of form is the world inhabited by beings who are free of the two desires of lust and food but still have material bodies, encompassing the eighteen heavens of the four meditations. The formless realm is the world inhabited by beings who are already without material bodies but abide with mind and consciousness in profound and wondrous meditative concentration, encompassing the four formless heavens (the heaven of boundless space, the heaven of boundless consciousness, the heaven of nothingness, and the heaven of neither perception nor non-perception). These three realms are all states of birth-and-death transmigration for ordinary beings.

[Since everything comes from the mind — not created in sequence, but through the karma made by each thought in our daily, present activity — one revolves through the ten dharma realms. If a single thought of greed, hatred, and delusion produces the ten evils — the three evils of body, four of speech, and three of mind — this becomes the cause of the painful destinies of the three lower paths. If a single thought turns the ten evils into the ten goods, this becomes the cause of the wondrous happiness of humans and devas. If a single thought forgets both good and evil, with no self seen within and no others seen without, and the one mind is serene and still, this becomes the cause of the śrāvaka's leaving suffering. If one contemplates the present pain and pleasure, adversity and success, as arising and ceasing through causes and conditions — the revolving of transmigration and the returning to cessation — this becomes the cause of the pratyekabuddha. If a single thought fully understands that persons and dharmas are without self, that causes and conditions are empty by nature, and that there is no doer and no receiver, yet without hindrance carries out the practices of the six perfections — giving, upholding precepts, and patience — to transform and deliver sentient beings, this becomes the cause of the bodhisattva. If a single thought suddenly awakens to one's own mind as originally bright and vast, embracing all things without exception, delivering all beings, with not a single dharma holding the mind, and sentient beings and Buddhas equal — this is the cause of becoming a Buddha.]
Although all dharmas are made by the mind, they are not created one after another as thoughts arise; rather, it is the karma made by each thought in our daily, present activity
that serves as the cause

, receiving its retribution while revolving through the ten dharma realms. If a single thought of greed, hatred, and delusion produces the ten evils (the three evils of body, four of speech, and three of mind), this is the cause of the painful destinies of the three lower paths. If a single thought turns the ten evils into the ten goods, this is the cause of the wondrous happiness of humans and devas. If a single thought forgets both good and evil, with no self seen within and no others seen without, and the one mind is serene and still, this is the cause of the śrāvaka's leaving suffering. If one contemplates the present pain and pleasure, adversity and success, as arising and ceasing through causes and conditions — the revolving of transmigration and the returning to cessation — this becomes the cause of the pratyekabuddha. If a single thought fully understands that persons and dharmas are without self, that causes and conditions are empty by nature, and that there is no doer and no receiver, yet without hindrance carries out the practices of the six perfections — giving, upholding precepts, and patience — to transform and deliver sentient beings, this becomes the cause of the bodhisattva. If a single thought suddenly awakens to one's own mind as originally bright and vast, embracing all things without exception, delivering all beings, utterly without the discriminating views of the emotional consciousness, with sentient beings and Buddhas equal and undivided — this is the cause of becoming a Buddha.

[The karma made] Karma is divided into collective karma and individual karma. Collective karma is the common karmic cause of sentient beings, which can summon the world of vessels — mountains, rivers, the great earth, and so on — shared in common by self and others; this is the karma of the circumstantial retribution. Individual karma is the karmic cause by which each individual sentient being summons its own retribution, such as differences in body and in pleasure and pain; this is the karma of the direct retribution. [Karma] All our wholesome and unwholesome thoughts, words, and deeds are called karma; wholesome thoughts, words, and deeds are called “wholesome karma,” and unwholesome thoughts, words, and deeds are called “unwholesome karma.” [Revolving transmigration and returning to cessation] Creating karma and receiving the fruits of birth and death is called revolving transmigration; cultivating the way and realizing nirvāṇa is called returning to cessation. “Returning to cessation” means returning to quiescence, that is, cultivating the way and realizing nirvāṇa.

[Therefore this one mind is vast and boundless, originally pure, perfect, and radiant. If in daily use you awaken to this in every thought, then even though you dwell amid the dust and toil of the world, you are a world-transcending person — this is why Vimalakīrti called it the non-dual Dharma gate. If you, good sir, can embody this and act upon it, then all gratitude and resentment, right and wrong, self and other, and the emotional roots of affliction will in a single thought transform into a treasury of radiant light. In every realm of daily life, try to observe in this way, and be aware in every thought. If you cannot bear it patiently and are obstructed by afflictions, then the moment you see them arise, immediately raise up the Sixth Patriarch's words ‘originally there is not a single thing’ like the vajra king's precious sword, and all afflictions will at once melt away like ice, and body and mind will turn into a pool of cool refreshment. If you practice thus with vigor and never retreat, you will at once realize the great field of liberation — what need is there to seek the Buddha-dharma anywhere else!]

Therefore this one mind is vast and boundless, originally pure, perfect, and radiant. If in daily use you awaken to this in every thought, then even though you dwell amid the dust and toil of the world, you are a world-transcending person — this is the non-dual Dharma gate spoken of in the Vimalakīrti Sutra. If you can embody this and act upon it, then all gratitude and resentment, right and wrong, self and other, and the emotional roots of affliction will in a single thought transform into a treasury of radiant light. In every realm of daily life, try to observe in this way, and be aware in every thought. If you cannot bear it patiently and are obstructed by afflictions, then the moment you see deluded thoughts arise, immediately raise up the Sixth Patriarch's words ‘originally there is not a single thing’ like the vajra king's precious sword, and all afflictions will at once melt away like ice, and body and mind will turn into a pool of cool refreshment. If you practice thus with vigor and never retreat, you will at once realize the great field of liberation — what need is there to seek the Buddha-dharma anywhere else!

[The non-dual Dharma gate] The teaching of the absolute, equal truth that transcends all relative distinctions — that which, above the eighty-four thousand Dharma gates of Buddhism, can directly reveal the holy path. The “Entering the Gate of Non-duality” chapter (chapter nine) of the Vimalakīrti Sutra records thirty-three kinds of non-dual Dharma gates. [Originally there is not a single thing] The Sixth Patriarch said: “Bodhi originally has no tree, the bright mirror also has no stand; originally there is not a single thing, where can dust alight?” (The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch). [The vajra king's precious sword] A sharp sword that severs all the entangling vines of emotional understanding. See the Record of Linji.
